name: channel-adapter
intent: Connect an application to a messaging channel without making the application a messaging client: an adapter acts as the client on the application's behalf, translating its own API, data and events into channel operations in both directions, so only the adapter knows the broker, the destinations and the wire format.
problem: An application that must send or receive messages has no messaging interface of its own, or must not grow one: its API, database or files predate the messaging system and its owners will not let it acquire broker dependencies. Writing messaging client calls into the application couples every call site to the messaging API - destinations, headers, serialization, acknowledgement - so the integration logic is duplicated across call sites, untestable without a broker, and impossible to replace when the transport or channel layout changes.
context: Applies at the seam between an application and a message channel - legacy or framework-bound applications joining an integration, services that must expose existing methods or events on a channel, or SDK/device boundaries whose native interface is a library API, a database or a file. The adapter is the only component that knows the messaging client, the wire format and the channel topology; the application keeps its own interface and data types.
benefits: The application stays messaging-agnostic: its interface and data types remain free of broker, destination and protocol concepts, and no call site contains client code.
Transport changes are local: moving from JMS to AMQP to Kafka, or changing the destination layout, means replacing one adapter per direction rather than editing the application.
Legacy systems participate without rework, because the adapter can attach at whichever layer of the architecture the required data or functionality already lives (API, database, file, event source).
Cross-cutting transport concerns - connection handling, reconnection, acknowledgement, serialization, headers, throughput limits - are centralised in one testable component.
The seam is independently replaceable in tests: a fake channel or a fake adapter lets application behaviour be exercised without a broker.
Cloud event bridges (EventBridge, CloudEvents) can normalise heterogeneous external event sources into a uniform channel contract, letting the application remain agnostic to SaaS event schemas.

The adapter boundary provides a natural chokepoint for observability: all cross-boundary messages pass through it, enabling latency histograms, error rate tracking and correlation without instrumentation in the application.
tradeoffs: A second contract to maintain: the adapter must track both the application interface and the messaging API/wire format, so every change on either side lands in it and it becomes a maintenance hotspot.

Delivery semantics are easy to assume away: because the application sees an ordinary method call, callers tend to assume synchronous, exactly-once, ordered behaviour that the channel does not provide - acknowledgement, redelivery and duplicate handling remain the adapter's implicit responsibility.
Adapters attract logic that does not belong to them: routing, transformation, retry and business rules accumulate until the adapter is an undeclared application layer with its own failure modes.
Extra hop and mapping cost: every call pays serialization plus the client library's overhead, which is a poor trade for chatty, latency-critical interactions that a direct call could serve.

Error translation is genuinely hard: mapping broker failures into application-meaningful errors (and vice versa) tends to either leak protocol exceptions or swallow them, and retry/idempotency policy ends up in the adapter by default.

Flow control must be handled deliberately: blocking adapters serialise the application behind a slow broker, and non-blocking clients silently buffer or drop messages unless the adapter honours backpressure.

CDC-based inbound adapters (Debezium, DynamoDB Streams) introduce operational complexity: a connector to run and monitor, schema evolution to manage, and a WAL/binlog reader that competes with existing replication load on the source database.

participants.responsibility: The existing application with its own interface and data model. It knows nothing about messaging channels, brokers or wire formats. It may expose an API, a database, a file system interface, or raise events via an existing mechanism.

A messaging client that consumes from a message channel and translates each message into an invocation of the application's interface. It owns deserialization, header mapping, correlation ID propagation and acknowledgement or rejection. It may be a polling adapter (periodically querying a source) or an event-driven adapter (subscribing to a stream or broker). Examples: SourcePollingChannelAdapter in Spring Integration; a Debezium inbound channel adapter; a Camel consumer component.

A messaging client that receives calls from the application and translates them into messages on a channel. It owns serialization, destination resolution, header enrichment, publisher confirms and error mapping. Examples: a @ServiceActivator-backed outbound channel adapter in Spring Integration; a Camel producer; a WSO2 broker-backed adapter.

The messaging system's channel abstraction: a named destination for messages, supporting point-to-point (queues) or publish-subscribe (topics) semantics. The adapter is the only component that names the channel directly; the application never references it.

use_cases: Exposing a legacy or batch application on a queue/topic without modifying its internals: one adapter reads its API or data and publishes, the reverse adapter invokes it for incoming traffic.
Publishing domain events from a service whose methods return data rather than messages (method call in, serialized event on the channel out).
Consuming commands from a broker and invoking existing service methods while keeping the service free of messaging types.
Bridging file- or database-driven applications into a messaging backbone: a polling adapter publishes new records, an outbound adapter appends incoming messages to the store.
Wrapping a third-party SDK, protocol library or device interface so that its events and commands appear as ordinary channel traffic.
Making an existing library usable synchronously and asynchronously by adding an adapter instead of changing the library's API.

Change Data Capture (CDC) polling: an inbound adapter periodically queries a database for new or changed rows (using timestamps, version columns or a change-log table) and publishes each change as a message, enabling legacy databases to participate in event-driven architectures without modifying the source system.

Cloud event ingestion: an inbound adapter polls a cloud queue (AWS SQS, Google Cloud Pub/Sub pull, Azure Service Bus) or subscribes to a cloud event source (EventBridge, CloudEvents HTTP push) and translates external events into the internal message format, bridging SaaS and PaaS event streams into the integration backbone.

IoT device gateway: an outbound adapter receives messages from the integration backbone and translates them into a device-specific protocol (MQTT, CoAP, HTTP), while an inbound adapter collects device telemetry and normalises it onto a channel, acting as the protocol translation boundary at the network edge.

Log-based CDC with Debezium: an inbound channel adapter runs a Debezium connector that tails the database write-ahead log (PostgreSQL WAL, MySQL binlog) and emits every committed row change as a message, providing ordered, lossless change capture without application-level polling or triggers.

Transactional outbox relay: an outbound adapter reads from an outbox table (written atomically with business data in the same DB transaction) and publishes to the broker, eliminating the dual-write problem for event-driven services without distributed transactions.

CloudEvents bridging: an inbound or outbound adapter transforms between the CloudEvents v1.0 specification (source, type, id, time, datacontenttype, dataschema, subject) and the internal message format, normalising event envelopes across heterogeneous cloud event sources and enabling interoperability with the CNCF CloudEvents standard.

Kafka Connect source and sink connectors as framework-managed channel adapters: a connector moves data between Kafka and an external system (JDBC database, S3, search index) with offset tracking, converter-based serialization, task parallelism and dead-letter routing owned by the Connect runtime, so neither the source nor the target system ever imports a Kafka client.

MicroProfile Reactive Messaging (Quarkus, SmallRye, Helidon): application beans consume and produce via @Incoming/@Outgoing methods on named channels while per-channel connectors (smallrye-kafka, MQTT, AMQP, Kinesis) act as inbound and outbound channel adapters, keeping transport client types out of business code.

Apache Camel components as catalog-shipped channel adapters: each component binds an external system (JMS, FTP, HTTP, databases, SaaS APIs) to the Camel message bus, so integration routes compose and reconfigure adapters declaratively instead of hand-writing client calls per endpoint.
avoid_when: The application already speaks the messaging API at every call site: the adapter adds a hop without removing any coupling.
Only one service method must be invoked per incoming message - a Service Activator or a plain Message Endpoint is the more specific fit.
The application-side interface is itself message-shaped; then a Messaging Gateway (a method call for the sender) is the right seam, not an adapter.
The real work is translating between two domain models; that is Message Translator / Canonical Data Model / Anti-Corruption Layer territory and a channel adapter alone will not solve it.
There is a single call site, a single transport and no expectation that either will change: a direct client call is simpler.

The integration requires exactly-once delivery semantics across the application boundary: the adapter alone cannot provide this; it requires the transactional outbox pattern combined with an idempotent consumer on the receiving side.
anti_patterns: The smart adapter: routing, transformation, retry and business rules accumulate until the adapter is an undeclared application layer with its own failure modes.
Leaking the messaging API through the application-facing interface (methods taking destinations or message objects), which reinstates the coupling the pattern removes.
Publishing without flow control: ignoring backpressure signals (a false return from channel.publish, no bounded buffer, blocking the event loop) and silently growing memory or dropping messages.
Treating the adapter as a transaction boundary: assuming that a returned method call means the message was delivered (no publisher confirms) and that a received message cannot be redelivered.
One adapter per call site or per message type instead of one per application interface, duplicating connection handling and serialization.
Polling without backoff on empty results: hammering a database or HTTP API with requests when no data is available, causing unnecessary load and throttling.
Absorbing exceptions silently: catching broker exceptions in the adapter without rethrowing, notifying the application, or moving the message to a dead-letter queue, so failures go unnoticed.

Embedding business transactions in the adapter: performing a database update and then publishing an event without an outbox pattern, creating a window where the update commits but the event is never published after a crash.

Event storm: an inbound adapter that saves to the database and triggers event subscribers in the same execution context, causing one incoming message to cascade into thousands of outgoing messages. Mitigation: disable subscriber scopes during data saves, or use source-tracking headers (x-source) to break bidirectional sync loops.

Bidirectional sync loop: two systems with outbound adapters publishing to each other via inbound adapters, each write triggering a cross-system event that loops forever. Mitigation: propagate source-identity headers; discard messages that originated from self.

Infinite retries without dead-letter: repeatedly failing messages are requeued forever, consuming broker resources and hiding the underlying failure. Mitigation: configure max retry attempts and a dead-letter destination for exhausted messages.

CDC adapter without idempotent consumers: a Debezium-based inbound adapter delivers every database change including on application-restart duplicates, and downstream consumers create duplicate records. Mitigation: idempotent consumer logic keyed on a stable business key, not the message ID.

Using message ID as idempotency key: some brokers (e.g., SQS redelivery) assign different message IDs on redelivery, making the key unstable. Mitigation: use a business-level idempotency key (order ID, entity ID + action + time bucket) combined with a conditional write or unique constraint.

Acknowledging before side effect: an inbound adapter acks a message before the application call completes, then crashes; the message is not redelivered but the effect never happened. Mitigation: process-then-ack, with idempotent side effects so replay is safe.

Outbox relay marking published before broker acknowledgement: the relay writes 'published' to the outbox row before the broker confirms receipt, so a crash between publish and mark-sent republishes the row as a duplicate. Mitigation: mark-sent only after the broker acknowledges, and emit the row with a monotonic sequence number so consumers can discard duplicates by ID.

Wrong move: relying on an adapter runtime's default fail-fast record handling (a Kafka Connect connector with errors.tolerance=none) -> a single malformed or poison record pauses the entire adapter and healthy traffic stops behind it -> instead set explicit error tolerance with a dead-letter destination and quarantine the poison record while the flow continues.

Wrong move: letting the adapter auto-register wire formats on first write in production (auto.register.schemas=true) -> an upstream field change silently breaks deserialization for every consumer and the adapter starts misreading data -> instead evolve schemas under registry compatibility checks and version the adapter's mapping deliberately.

Wrong move: scaling the adapter by adding instances or tasks without checking that its work is parallelisable -> a single-table source or a rate-limited external API gains no throughput and worker churn only adds rebalance gaps -> instead match parallelism to independently parallelisable units of work and fix the true bottleneck (partitioning, sink limits, broker capacity) first.
design_principles: Dependency inversion: the application depends on its own interface; the adapter and the messaging API depend on that interface.
Separation of concerns: transport and protocol mechanics are isolated from application behaviour.
Single responsibility: one adapter per application interface and direction, doing translation only.
Information hiding: destinations, headers, wire formats and client objects stay behind the adapter.
Interface segregation: inbound (message-to-application) and outbound (application-to-message) adapters stay separate so neither side inherits unused operations.
Idempotent inbound processing: the receiver must handle duplicate messages gracefully since distributed messaging guarantees at-least-once delivery.

Dual-write avoidance: outbound adapters must never write business data and publish a message in separate operations; use the transactional outbox pattern to make them atomically co-committed with the business data.
Backpressure propagation: an adapter must surface broker or downstream backpressure to the calling application rather than buffering unboundedly.
Observable boundary: all messages cross the application boundary through the adapter, making it the natural place to emit latency, error rate and throughput metrics.
best_practices: Define the application-facing interface first; the adapter implements or consumes it and never exposes broker types in it.
Keep the adapter thin: delegate payload mapping to translators/mappers, routing to routers/filters, and error policy to the application or a dedicated messaging layer.
Make delivery semantics explicit - acknowledgement mode, publisher confirms, idempotency, duplicate handling, ordering - and document them at the boundary.
Manage the connection lifecycle: reconnection, resubscription, draining and shutdown, with in-flight handlers awaited or requeued rather than abandoned.
Apply bounded prefetch and buffers, and propagate backpressure into the application path instead of buffering without limit.
Enforce security at the seam: credentials/TLS configuration, payload validation and least-privilege destinations live in the adapter.
Correlate across the boundary (message id and correlation id headers) so an application-level operation can be traced into and out of the channel.
Test the adapter against a fake channel (in-memory implementation of the messaging port) and cover broker-down, malformed-message and redelivery paths.
For inbound polling adapters: always return null when no data is available, configure max-messages-per-poll explicitly, and use exponential backoff on empty results to avoid hammering slow back-ends.
Implement idempotent receive using a deduplication key (message id or business key) stored in a bounded cache or database with TTL, so duplicate deliveries do not cause duplicate side effects.

Use the outbox pattern for outbound adapters that must atomically persist application state and publish an event: write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction, and relay it to the broker asynchronously via polling or CDC.
Integrate a circuit breaker between the adapter and unreliable external systems (HTTP APIs, legacy DBs) so a cascade of failures does not destabilise the messaging runtime.
Expose operational metrics (messages processed, publish latency, error rate, queue depth) from the adapter so integration health can be monitored independently of the application.

For CDC-based inbound adapters (Debezium, DynamoDB Streams): configure the snapshot mode explicitly (prefer 'initial' for new pipelines, 'always' for restart-safe pipelines); protect the schema-history topic from deletion; and set REPLICA IDENTITY FULL on PostgreSQL tables to capture before-images on updates and deletes.

Use CloudEvents v1.0 as the canonical outbound envelope when bridging to cloud-native event routers (AWS EventBridge, Azure Event Grid, Google Cloud Eventarc): map source, id, type, time, subject, datacontenttype and dataschema correctly so cloud consumers receive a standards-compliant event.

For IoT device adapters: distinguish between MQTT/CoAP QoS levels and map them to channel acknowledgement semantics; CoAP observe relationships must be re-established on reconnect; device command adapters should use a command-ID header so devices can idempotently discard duplicate commands.

Classify dead-letter outcomes explicitly: transient failures (network timeout) merit retry with backoff; validation failures merit zero retries and immediate DLQ placement; poison messages (malformed but repeated) merit quarantine and manual inspection. Never let failed messages accumulate in the DLQ without alerting.

Prevent event storms by disabling subscriber scopes during data-persist operations in the application; or by propagating source-identity headers (x-source) so that inbound adapters discard messages that originated from the same system.

For Debezium CDC adapters: prefer the Outbox Event Router SMT (Single Message Transform) to route outbox events to topic-per-aggregate-type rather than emitting raw database-change events, giving consumers a clean domain event envelope instead of a row-diff envelope.

When the adapter bridges a transactional system (e.g., a database) and a message broker, prefer atomic co-commit via the transactional outbox + CDC relay over application-level dual-writes, which cannot be made atomic without distributed transactions.
